Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Olympic swimming champion Michael Phelps will not face criminal charges in connection with a November party at which he was photographed using a bong, a South Carolina sheriff said Monday. Michael Phelps admitted "regrettable behavior" after a  photo of him using a bong was published. "We do not believe we have enough evidence to prosecute anyone" who was at the party in Columbia, South Carolina, Richland County Sheriff Leon Lott told reporters, adding that authorities are ending their investigation into Phelps. "We had a photo, and we had him saying he was sorry for his inappropriate behavior," Lott said. "That behavior could have been going to a party. ... He never said, 'I smoked marijuana.' He never confessed to that. We didn't have physical evidence. We didn't have enough where we could go arrest him." Phelps, 23, who won a record eight gold medals at the 2008 Olympic Games in Beijing, China, admitted "regrettable behavior" after a British newspaper published the photograph about two weeks ago. The tabloid News of the World showed Phelps using the bong during what it said was a November party at the University of South Carolina in Columbia.  Watch the sheriff say he won't prosecute Phelps » . A bong is a device commonly used to smoke marijuana. University police and Columbia police both said they would not pursue charges against Phelps. Lott said he has not spoken to Phelps, but hopes the swimming champion has learned from his mistakes and is willing to share an anti-drug message with children. Phelps said Monday he had learned some "important lessons" from the incident. "I'm glad this matter is put to rest," he said in a written statement. "But there are also some important lessons that I've learned. For me, it's all about recognizing that I used bad judgment and it's a mistake I won't make again. For young people especially -- be careful about the decisions you make. One bad decision can really hurt you and the people you care about. "I really appreciate the support my family and fans have shown me, and now I will move forward and dive back into the pool, having put this whole thing behind me."  Watch Phelps acknowledge making 'a mistake' » . Phelps told CNN affiliate WBAL in Baltimore, Maryland, "This is something that I need to learn from, will learn from and have learned from." "I know that a lot of people make mistakes, and the best way to learn from them is changing things," Phelps told WBAL. Lott said the photo that surfaced of Phelps put him and his department in a "no-win situation." If he had ignored it, he said, he would have faced criticism, but he also was criticized for investigating. However, he said, the photo did initiate an investigation into goings-on at the home where the party took place, and some people were arrested on suspicion of drug possession. The home has been the focus of previous drug-related investigations, he said. He defended his investigation, saying, "As a cop, my responsibility is to enforce the law, not to create it or ignore it. Marijuana in the state of South Carolina is illegal."

(CNN) — Michael Phelps, the Olympic swimming champion, will not be charged over a November party in Columbia, South Carolina, where a photograph appeared to show him using a bong, Richland County Sheriff Leon Lott announced Monday.

Lott said investigators were closing the case because there was insufficient evidence to prosecute Phelps or anyone else who attended the gathering. According to the sheriff, authorities had only the photograph and Phelps’ apology for what the swimmer described as inappropriate conduct. Phelps never specifically acknowledged smoking marijuana, and investigators found no physical evidence that would justify an arrest, Lott explained.

The 23-year-old athlete, who set a record by winning eight gold medals at the 2008 Olympics in Beijing, China, admitted to behavior he regretted after the image was published by a British newspaper roughly two weeks earlier. The tabloid News of the World reported that the picture showed Phelps using a bong at a November party near the University of South Carolina in Columbia. A bong is an apparatus frequently associated with smoking marijuana. Video footage featured the sheriff explaining why Phelps would not be prosecuted.

Neither the University of South Carolina police nor the Columbia Police Department planned to bring charges against the swimmer.

Although Lott said he had not personally spoken with Phelps, he expressed hope that the Olympic champion had learned from the episode and might help deliver an anti-drug message to children.

In a written statement Monday, Phelps said the experience had taught him significant lessons and that he was relieved the matter had been resolved. He acknowledged exercising poor judgment, promised not to repeat the mistake, and warned young people to think carefully about their choices because a single bad decision can harm both them and those close to them. Phelps also thanked his family and fans for supporting him and said he intended to leave the controversy behind and return his attention to swimming. Video also showed him recognizing that he had made a mistake.

Speaking with CNN affiliate WBAL in Baltimore, Maryland, Phelps said the incident was something from which he needed to learn, would learn, and already had learned. He added that many people make mistakes and that the most effective way to learn from them is to change one’s behavior.

Lott described the publication of the photograph as placing both him and his department in an impossible position. He said officials would have been criticized for disregarding the image, yet they also received criticism for opening an investigation.

The inquiry nevertheless led authorities to examine activity at the house where the party reportedly occurred. Several individuals were arrested on suspicion of possessing drugs, and Lott said the residence had previously been investigated in connection with drug activity.

Defending the decision to investigate, Lott said his duty as a law-enforcement officer was to uphold existing laws rather than make or disregard them. He emphasized that marijuana is illegal in South Carolina.

# Michael Phelps will not face charges over photo appearing to show marijuana use

**COLUMBIA, South Carolina** — Olympic swimming champion Michael Phelps will not face criminal charges stemming from a photograph that appeared to show him inhaling from a marijuana pipe at a South Carolina party, the Richland County sheriff said.

Sheriff Leon Lott said investigators had pursued leads connected to the photograph but did not have enough evidence to prosecute Phelps.

“We do not believe we have enough evidence to prosecute anyone, including Michael Phelps,” Lott said in announcing the decision.

The image, first published by the British tabloid *News of the World*, appeared to show Phelps holding a glass pipe commonly used to smoke marijuana. The newspaper said the photograph was taken at a party near the University of South Carolina in November 2008, several months after Phelps won a record eight gold medals at the Beijing Olympics.

Phelps acknowledged attending the party and apologized for his conduct, though his public statement did not explicitly say that he had used marijuana.

“I engaged in behavior which was regrettable and demonstrated bad judgment,” Phelps said. “I’m 23 years old, and despite the successes I’ve had in the pool, I acted in a youthful and inappropriate way, not in a manner people have come to expect from me.”

“For this, I am sorry,” he added. “I promise my fans and the public — it will not happen again.”

Lott said his department had an obligation to investigate because the alleged incident occurred within its jurisdiction. But the sheriff emphasized that a photograph and reports about a party were not enough, by themselves, to establish a criminal case beyond a reasonable doubt.

Authorities did not recover marijuana from Phelps, did not conduct a drug test at the time of the alleged incident and lacked direct physical evidence tying him to possession of the drug, according to the sheriff’s explanation.

Lott also rejected suggestions that Phelps had received preferential treatment because of his celebrity.

“Michael Phelps is truly an American hero,” the sheriff said, but added that the swimmer would be treated like anyone else under the law. The investigation, Lott said, was intended to determine whether admissible evidence existed—not to single out Phelps because of his fame.

Phelps became one of the world’s most recognizable athletes after his performance in Beijing, where he surpassed Mark Spitz’s record of seven gold medals at a single Olympic Games. His success brought him lucrative endorsement deals and positioned him as a prominent role model, especially for young swimmers.

The photograph nevertheless produced swift consequences outside the criminal justice system. USA Swimming suspended Phelps from competition for three months, saying the action was intended to send a strong message about his responsibilities as a public figure. The organization said the suspension was not based on an anti-doping violation.

Kellogg also announced that it would not renew its endorsement agreement with Phelps, saying his behavior was inconsistent with the company’s image. Other sponsors continued to support him.

Phelps said he accepted responsibility for his actions and intended to learn from the episode. The swimmer had faced controversy before: In 2004, he pleaded guilty to driving while impaired in Maryland and received probation.

The South Carolina decision ended the immediate possibility of prosecution over the party photograph. Lott said that while investigators took the allegation seriously, criminal charges require evidence that can stand up in court.

The sheriff’s announcement meant Phelps would avoid a legal case, but the incident remained a significant public setback for an athlete whose Olympic achievements had made him an international symbol of discipline and success.
